Instructor demonstration: Learn PostgreSQL Tutorial - Full Course for Beginners, 03:29:30-03:40:53. Watch
inner and left joins. Our own fixtures include unmatched customers and an empty order. Stop manually at the
listed end. Public YouTube title, creator, runtime and expanded publisher chapter list inspected. No full-playback
or transcript-completeness claim.
Why this matters, and what you will do
M02 kept one item per order in a simplified table. Real systems often store customers, orders
and order items separately. You will attach a customer name to each order without losing track
of unmatched records. Complete M02, keep the loaded course schema, and use course.orders
and course.customers for this lesson. They are new training tables; order IDs begin with O rather
than the M02 numeric-looking IDs.
A join combines records according to a matching condition. A key identifies a record or links it
to another table. Here customers has one row per customer, identified by customer_id. orders
has one row per order, identified by order_id, and may refer to a customer_id. These fields have
different roles: several orders can belong to one customer.
Picture it before writing it
Asha's customer card is C01. Orders O101 and O103 both refer to C01, so both may legitimately
display Asha after a join. The two displayed names do not mean the customer table contains
duplicate Asha cards. O106 has no customer_id; we have an order but no customer identity for
it. Tara, C05, has no order in the training source.
Question
Appropriate starting point
Expected grain
Orders with a matched
customer
orders joined to customers
One row per matched order
Every order, named if
possible
orders LEFT JOIN customers
One row per order here
Every customer, with any
orders
customers LEFT JOIN orders
One row per customer/order match, plus
unmatched customer
The last result is not necessarily one row per customer because Asha has two orders. Predicting
that multiplicity is the next lesson's main work.
Follow with me once
SELECT o.order_id, c.customer_name, o.shipping_fee
FROM course.orders AS o
INNER JOIN course.customers AS c
ON o.customer_id = c.customer_id
ORDER BY o.order_id;
AS o and AS c give the tables short names within this query. o.order_id means the order_id
belonging to o. ON states the matching relationship. INNER JOIN keeps matched pairs. The
output is O101 Asha/20, O102 Ravi/10, O103 Asha/0, O104 Mina/15 and O105 Iqbal/5. Five rows
appear; O106 is excluded because its null customer_id does not match a known customer key.
Now preserve every order:
SELECT o.order_id, o.customer_id, c.customer_name
FROM course.orders AS o
LEFT JOIN course.customers AS c
ON o.customer_id = c.customer_id
ORDER BY o.order_id;
Six rows appear. O106 has a NULL name as well as its NULL customer_id. LEFT JOIN preserves
each left-side row, with right-side nulls if there is no match. It does not promise exactly one
output per left row when several matches exist. Here customer_id is unique in customers, so
each order matches at most one customer.
ON versus WHERE can change preservation
Suppose you want every order and an East-region customer name where one matches. Put the
right-side restriction inside the matching rule:
SELECT o.order_id, c.customer_name
FROM course.orders AS o
LEFT JOIN course.customers AS c
ON o.customer_id = c.customer_id
AND c.region = 'East'
ORDER BY o.order_id;
All six orders remain, but only O101, O102 and O103 get names. If instead you put WHERE
c.region = 'East' after the join, the null-extended rows fail that filter, and only those three orders
remain. Neither form is automatically wrong; they answer different questions. State which
records must be preserved before choosing where to put the condition.
If you are stuck
“Column customer_id is ambiguous” means the name exists on both sides and PostgreSQL
needs you to identify which one. Prefix it with o. or c. An unexpectedly large result can mean the
ON condition is missing or matches non-unique values. Do not join customer names merely
because they look readable; names can repeat or change. Use the declared relationship key.
Your independent practice
Start with all customers and attach their order IDs using LEFT JOIN. Display customer_id,
customer_name and order_id, sorted by customer_id and order_id. Predict how many rows Asha
produces and what Tara's order field shows.
Changed retry - after your first review
Return every order but attach a customer name only when the customer belongs to North. Keep
all original orders, including those outside North and O106. Explain why WHERE region = 'North'
would fail that preservation rule.
Ready-made revision
INNER JOIN keeps matching pairs. LEFT JOIN also preserves unmatched left rows. Use the
relationship key, qualify ambiguous names and predict multiplicity. ON defines matches; WHERE
can remove rows after the join. Record both row counts and unmatched cases, not only a
familiar-looking name.
Evidence to keep: your attempt, the observed result and its explanation. Save the first attempt before
opening DE03-01 in the Explained Reviews book. After review, solve the changed retry and keep it as a

Before starting: DE03-01. Video: Instructor watch ranges appear below. Read the vocabulary, perform
the guided example and save an independent attempt before review.
Instructor demonstration: Learn SQL Beginner to Advanced in Under 4 Hours, 51:10-01:08:04. Optional joins
refresher after stating both input grains. Our book explicitly demonstrates row multiplication and proves the
corrected totals; the video is not a replacement for that validation. Stop manually at the listed end. Public
YouTube title, creator, runtime and expanded publisher chapter list inspected. No full-playback or
transcript-completeness claim.
Why this matters, and what you will do
A silent join error can multiply an order's shipping fee without producing any SQL error. You will
identify each table's grain, predict a one-to-many join, measure the multiplication, and choose a
repair that respects what each amount represents. Complete DE03-01.
Cardinality describes how many matches a relationship permits. Fan-out is the multiplication
of a left record across several matching right records. An invariant is a fact expected to remain
true across a transformation, such as the total fee attached once to each original order. A
composite key identifies a record using more than one field together.
course.order_items has one row per order line. Its key is (order_id, line_no). O101 has two lines:
two notebooks amounting to 99, and three pens amounting to 30. Its order-level shipping fee is
20. The correct combined amount is 99 + 30 + 20 = 149. The fee belongs to the whole order,
not independently to each line.
Predict the shape first
There are six orders, eight item lines and five distinct order IDs represented in items. O106 has
no item lines. An INNER JOIN from orders to items therefore produces eight matched line rows
and drops O106. A LEFT JOIN produces those eight line rows plus one null-extended O106 row:
nine results. The left join retains every order but does not preserve the original six-row grain.
Follow with me once
SELECT o.order_id, i.line_no,
i.quantity * i.unit_price AS item_amount,
o.shipping_fee
FROM course.orders AS o
JOIN course.order_items AS i
ON o.order_id = i.order_id
ORDER BY o.order_id, i.line_no;
Look at O101's two rows: each displays shipping_fee 20. That repetition is expected at line
grain. It becomes a financial error only if you add the fee as though each displayed copy were a
separate charge. A joined field can be safe to display and unsafe to sum at the new grain.
SELECT COUNT(*) AS joined_rows,
COUNT(DISTINCT o.order_id) AS represented_orders,
SUM(o.shipping_fee) AS repeated_fees
FROM course.orders AS o
JOIN course.order_items AS i
ON o.order_id = i.order_id;
SELECT COUNT(*) AS source_orders,
SUM(shipping_fee) AS source_fees
FROM course.orders;
The joined summary is 8 rows, 5 represented orders and 75 repeated fees. The original is 6
orders and 50 fees. O101 adds one extra 20 and O105 adds one extra 5, so the sum is inflated
by 25. O106's omitted fee happens to be zero; the fee-total comparison alone would not reveal
its lost order. That is why row coverage and amount reconciliation are separate checks.
Repair the grain, not the appearance
For one order, aggregate item values first and attach its fee once:
SELECT o.order_id, o.shipping_fee,
(SELECT SUM(i.quantity * i.unit_price)
FROM course.order_items AS i
WHERE i.order_id = o.order_id) AS item_total
FROM course.orders AS o
WHERE o.order_id = 'O101';
The result has one O101 row, fee 20 and item_total 129. Its payable amount is 149. This is a
correlated subquery: the inner query uses the outer order ID. DE03-06 explains that mechanism;
DE03-07 builds a more reusable all-order version with a CTE. Here the important repair is
producing item totals at order grain before combining order-level measures.
SUM(DISTINCT shipping_fee) is not that repair. It removes repeated equal fee values across
different orders too. If two genuine orders each paid 10, a distinct sum would count 10 once
instead of 20. An amount is not an order key.
Other join shapes you should recognise
A RIGHT JOIN preserves the right side; reversing table positions and using LEFT JOIN often
expresses the same intent more readably. FULL OUTER JOIN preserves unmatched records from
both sides. Those can help reconcile independent deliveries, but matching duplicates still
multiply pairs. A CROSS JOIN pairs every left row with every right row: six orders and five
customers make thirty pairs. Use that only when every combination is the intended result, not
as a substitute for a missing ON condition.
Your independent practice
Inspect O105's item lines. Calculate its item total and correct fee-inclusive amount by hand,
then use a query to verify the item total. Calculate the wrong fee-inclusive amount produced by
adding its fee once per item line. State the grain of that wrong intermediate result.
Changed retry - after your first review
Count all rows from a LEFT JOIN of orders to items. Also count non-null item line numbers and
distinct order IDs. Explain why these three counts differ, and identify the row causing the
difference between the first two counts.
Ready-made revision
Declare both input grains, matching keys, expected cardinality and final grain. Count source
rows, joined rows, represented keys and unmatched cases. Aggregate line measures to order
grain before adding order-level charges. DISTINCT on a money value cannot replace a
key-aware repair.

Instructor demonstration: Learn SQL Beginner to Advanced in Under 4 Hours, 01:08:04-01:15:10. Watch
UNION. Our lesson explains UNION ALL, duplicate meaning and introduces INTERSECT/EXCEPT. Stop manually at
the listed end. Public YouTube title, creator, runtime and expanded publisher chapter list inspected. No
full-playback or transcript-completeness claim.
Why this matters, and what you will do
Joins attach related fields side by side. Sometimes you need to append compatible records from
two deliveries instead. You will use UNION ALL to preserve occurrences and UNION when the
question asks for unique selected rows. Complete DE03-02.
A set operation combines query results vertically. Each branch must return the same number
of columns in the corresponding order, with compatible types. Output labels come from the first
branch. Picture putting two receipt stacks on top of each other. That operation is different from
attaching a customer's name to a receipt.
Follow with me once
SELECT order_id, category
FROM course.sales
WHERE ordered_on = DATE '2026-09-01'
UNION ALL
SELECT order_id, category
FROM course.sales
WHERE ordered_on = DATE '2026-09-02'
ORDER BY order_id;
Four rows remain: 0007 Paper, 0008 Writing, 0009 Paper and 0010 Writing. UNION ALL retains
every occurrence from both branches. The final ORDER BY applies to the combined result.
Neither branch needs a separate ORDER BY for this question.
Now select only category and use UNION:
SELECT category FROM course.sales
WHERE ordered_on = DATE '2026-09-01'
UNION
SELECT category FROM course.sales
WHERE ordered_on = DATE '2026-09-02'
ORDER BY category;
Only Paper and Writing remain because UNION removes duplicate whole output rows. If UNION
ALL were used with those category-only branches, Paper would appear twice and Writing twice.
Neither version deletes anything from course.sales. They request different result shapes.
A duplicate occurrence can be legitimate
Two sales of Pen are two sales, not automatically one duplicated event. If a daily ingestion
replays the same order_id by mistake, you need a business key and a chosen replay policy to
repair it. UNION on a truncated list of fields may collapse legitimate events, while including a
delivery timestamp could keep replayed events distinct. Think about identity before using an
operation that discards rows.
You can add a literal source label to retain provenance:
SELECT 'day_1' AS source_batch, order_id
FROM course.sales
WHERE ordered_on = DATE '2026-09-01'
UNION ALL
SELECT 'day_2' AS source_batch, order_id
FROM course.sales
WHERE ordered_on = DATE '2026-09-02'
ORDER BY source_batch, order_id;
The label lets you trace which branch supplied a result. It is an original query value, not a field
that already existed in the table. Because it becomes part of the selected row, it also affects
uniqueness if you later change UNION ALL to UNION.
Related operations
INTERSECT returns selected rows common to both results. EXCEPT returns selected rows from
the first result absent from the second. Their default forms remove duplicate rows; ALL variants
have multiplicity rules that are outside this first lesson. For now, use them on small key lists you
can inspect. They compare output rows, not a hidden matching condition like a JOIN's ON clause.
If you are stuck
An unequal-column error means the branches disagree about their output shape. Compare both
field lists in order. Compatible types are not enough for compatible meanings: a numeric unit
price placed under a quantity heading would still be wrong. Do not fix a type problem by turning
every value into text without deciding what that shared output column represents.
Your independent practice
Append the category values from course.practice_sales on October 1 and October 2 using
UNION ALL. Repeat with UNION. Predict both row counts and explain which repeated category is
removed in the second result.
Changed retry - after your first review
Find categories appearing in course.retry_sales on both November 1 and November 2 using
INTERSECT. Then find categories from November 1 absent on November 2 using EXCEPT.
Ready-made revision
JOIN combines matching records side by side; UNION operations append compatible result rows.
UNION ALL preserves occurrences, UNION removes duplicates of the whole selected row. Align
column meaning and type. Preserve source labels when provenance matters, and distinguish
legitimate repeated values from replayed business events.

Before starting: DE03-03. Video: Instructor watch ranges appear below. Read the vocabulary, perform
the guided example and save an independent attempt before review.
Instructor demonstration: Learn SQL Beginner to Advanced in Under 4 Hours, 01:15:10-01:26:39. Watch
string functions; Alex uses MySQL. PostgreSQL uses LENGTH, TRIM and SUBSTRING forms shown in our book;
there is no native MySQL-style LOCATE or IFNULL to copy. Stop manually at the listed end. Public YouTube title,
creator, runtime and expanded publisher chapter list inspected. No full-playback or transcript-completeness
claim.
Why this matters, and what you will do
In M02 you trimmed ordinary surrounding spaces and changed case. You will now treat blank
cleaned labels as missing, inspect the transformation and avoid inventing a product identity
from similar-looking text. Complete DE03-03. Cleaning is a controlled rule, not a command to
make every string look alike.
Standardisation converts known variants into a consistent representation. Normalisation can
mean several things in computing; in this lesson it means a text-formatting rule, not relational
database normalisation. Provenance means knowing where a value came from and how it
changed. A mapping is an explicit association between a source label and a known target
value.
Follow with me once
SELECT source_id, item_raw,
LENGTH(item_raw) AS raw_length,
NULLIF(LOWER(TRIM(item_raw)), '') AS item_clean
FROM course.raw_labels
ORDER BY source_id;
A's raw length is 6 and its clean value is pen. B's length is 3 and its clean value is pen. C's length
is 0 and its clean value is NULL. D has null length and null clean value. E has length 11 and
cleans to note book. F has length 9 and keeps pen blue with two internal spaces. Inspect these
alongside the raw values rather than trusting a visual glance at blank-looking cells.
Read the nested expression from the inside out: TRIM removes surrounding spaces; LOWER
changes case; NULLIF compares that cleaned result with the empty string and returns NULL
when they are equal. If the raw input is already NULL, it remains missing through this
expression. The empty string is written as two single quotes with nothing between them.
Validate the effect of the rule
SELECT COUNT(*) AS raw_rows,
COUNT(item_raw) AS raw_non_null,
COUNT(NULLIF(LOWER(TRIM(item_raw)), ''))
AS usable_clean_labels
FROM course.raw_labels;
There are six raw rows, five non-null raw labels and four usable non-blank cleaned labels. One
empty string became explicitly missing; the original NULL stayed missing. Cleaning did not
reduce the source row count. If you later filter to only usable labels, that deliberate rejection
step should be counted and explained separately.
A pattern match is not proof of identity
SELECT source_id, item_raw
FROM course.raw_labels
WHERE LOWER(TRIM(item_raw)) LIKE 'pen%'
ORDER BY source_id;
A, B and F match. The % wildcard means zero or more following characters. It catches pen and
pen blue, which may represent different products. LIKE is useful for finding candidates to
inspect; it does not prove those candidates share one product key. An underscore wildcard
means one character, so literal wildcard characters require deliberate escaping when that
situation arises.
Removing every internal space would turn note book into notebook, but it would also change
other labels indiscriminately. Use a reviewed lookup mapping if you know that a particular
spelling refers to a particular product. Preserve an unmapped category when you do not know.
The same caution applies to replacing punctuation, stripping leading zeros from IDs or merging
differently cased identifiers whose system treats case as meaningful.
If you are stuck
Check LENGTH and the raw value to distinguish empty from null. TRIM's ordinary-space rule may
not remove tabs or non-breaking spaces; do not claim universal whitespace repair. If two raw
labels now share one clean value, inspect whether that collision is expected. A standardised
display label is not necessarily a unique identifier.
Your independent practice
Return only source IDs whose cleaned label under the guided rule is missing. Keep the raw label
in the result. Then count distinct non-null cleaned labels and explain why that count is lower
than the number of usable cleaned rows.
Changed retry - after your first review
Using only the three literal inputs below, calculate raw value, cleaned value and cleaned length:
' Bag ', 'BAG' and ' '. You can use UNION ALL to create three SELECT statements. Decide whether
a blank cleaned value should have length zero or a null length under the chosen missing-label
rule.
Ready-made revision
Keep raw data and describe each cleaning rule. NULLIF(TRIM(...), '') can represent blank labels
as missing. Count raw rows, usable values and unique cleaned values separately. Pattern
matches identify candidates, not reliable product identity. Do not erase unknown mappings or
leading zeros to make data look tidy.

Before starting: DE03-04. Video: Instructor watch ranges appear below. Read the vocabulary, perform
the guided example and save an independent attempt before review.
Instructor demonstration: SQL for Data Analytics - Learn SQL in 4 Hours, 02:10:02-02:20:26. Watch date/time
functions. The book supplies the India/UTC boundary example and half-open timestamp filter. Stop manually at
the listed end. Public YouTube title, creator, runtime and expanded publisher chapter list inspected. No
full-playback or transcript-completeness claim.
Why this matters, and what you will do
A sale close to midnight can belong to one day in India and a different day in UTC. You will
distinguish a calendar date from an instant, select a local business day with exact boundaries
and avoid missing the last second of a reporting period. Complete DE03-04.
A date is a calendar day. A timestamp without time zone is a date and clock reading without
a uniquely specified global instant. PostgreSQL timestamptz represents an instant and displays
it in the session's time zone; it does not retain the original named zone supplied by the source.
UTC is a shared time reference. AT TIME ZONE can convert a timestamptz instant to the local
clock reading for a chosen zone.
Picture the boundary
The three events in course.events are chosen around midnight in India. Their instants are T1 at
August 31 18:30 UTC, T2 at September 1 18:29:59 UTC, and T3 one second later. At
Asia/Kolkata, those are September 1 00:00, September 1 23:59:59 and September 2 00:00. The
same instants have different calendar labels depending on the zone used for the question.
Follow with me once
SELECT event_id,
happened_at AT TIME ZONE 'UTC' AS utc_clock,
happened_at AT TIME ZONE 'Asia/Kolkata' AS india_clock,
(happened_at AT TIME ZONE 'Asia/Kolkata')::date
AS india_date
FROM course.events
ORDER BY happened_at;
The ::date suffix casts the local clock reading to its calendar date. This is PostgreSQL cast
syntax; CAST(expression AS date) is another form. The timezone conversion happens before the
date extraction, so the date refers to the intended business location rather than your session
default.
Filter one full local day
SELECT event_id
FROM course.events
WHERE happened_at >= TIMESTAMPTZ '2026-09-01 00:00:00+05:30'
AND happened_at < TIMESTAMPTZ '2026-09-02 00:00:00+05:30'
ORDER BY happened_at;
T1 and T2 qualify; T3 is excluded at the next day's exact boundary. The +05:30 offset is
appropriate for these India dates. Other regions may have daylight-saving changes, so do not
assume every local calendar day everywhere contains exactly 24 hours or that one fixed offset
is valid all year. Naming the reporting zone makes the requirement clear.
Do not use BETWEEN September 1 midnight AND September 2 midnight for this full-day rule:
BETWEEN includes both boundaries and would also include T3. Do not use an imagined last
instant of 23:59:59, because real timestamps can contain fractional seconds after it. Inclusive
start and exclusive next start handles those records cleanly.
Group by the reporting period
SELECT
(happened_at AT TIME ZONE 'Asia/Kolkata')::date AS day,
COUNT(*) AS events
FROM course.events
GROUP BY (happened_at AT TIME ZONE 'Asia/Kolkata')::date
ORDER BY day;
September 1 has two events and September 2 has one. Counts reconcile to three input events.
For month-level summaries, DATE_TRUNC('month', local_clock) returns the beginning of the
month as a period label. That is a bucket label, not the original event timestamp. Preserve the
raw instant when detail-level investigation matters.
Recovery and validation
If a timestamp displays differently on another computer, check the session time zone before
assuming the stored instant changed. SHOW TIME ZONE displays the session setting. The
explicit conversions above make the displayed comparisons stable regardless of that setting. If
a timestamp source lacks an offset or known zone, do not guess one silently; obtain its source
convention before treating it as an instant.
Your independent practice
Select the India calendar day September 2 from course.events using explicit timestamptz
boundaries. Predict which event sits exactly on its beginning. Save the SQL and explain why that
event was excluded from the preceding day's query.
Changed retry - after your first review
Select September 1 according to UTC instead of India. Then explain why a different pair of IDs is
correct despite the stored events being unchanged.
Ready-made revision
A calendar date, local clock reading and global instant are different things. State the reporting
zone, convert before extracting a local date, and use inclusive-start/exclusive-end windows. Test
a record at the beginning, just before the end and exactly at the next beginning. Reconcile
grouped counts to the included events.
Evidence to keep: your attempt, the observed result and its explanation. Save the first attempt before
opening DE03-05 in the Explained Reviews book. After review, solve the changed retry and keep it as a

Before starting: DE03-05. Video: Instructor watch ranges appear below. Read the vocabulary, perform
the guided example and save an independent attempt before review.
Instructor demonstration: Learn SQL Beginner to Advanced in Under 4 Hours, 01:35:16-01:45:58. Revisit the
subquery visual with this lesson's deeper scalar-cardinality and EXISTS questions. Do not repeat the full video if
the earlier watch is clear. Stop manually at the listed end. Public YouTube title, creator, runtime and expanded
publisher chapter list inspected. No full-playback or transcript-completeness claim.
Why this matters, and what you will do
You have used a scalar average inside a query. Now you will ask a different question: “Which
customers have at least one paid order?” The answer should contain each customer once, even
if that customer has several paid orders. You will use correlated EXISTS and NOT EXISTS to
express that purpose directly. Complete DE03-05.
A correlated subquery refers to the current outer row. In c.customer_id = o.customer_id, c
may belong to the outer query and o to the inner query. You can picture the outer customer
holding up an ID while the smaller query checks the order stack for a match. This is a reasoning
model; it is not a promise that the engine physically rescans the whole order table for each
customer.
Follow with me once
SELECT c.customer_id, c.customer_name
FROM course.customers AS c
WHERE EXISTS (
SELECT 1
FROM course.orders AS o
WHERE o.customer_id = c.customer_id
AND o.is_paid = TRUE
ORDER BY c.customer_id;
C01 Asha and C04 Iqbal qualify. Asha has two paid orders, O101 and O103, but appears once
because the outer source has one row per customer and EXISTS returns only a yes/no decision
for each. An INNER JOIN to paid orders would produce three matched rows before any further
grouping: two Asha rows and one Iqbal row. The choice depends on the requested grain.
The line o.customer_id = c.customer_id is essential. If you remove it, the inner query merely
asks whether any paid order exists anywhere. That answer is true for this database, so all five
customers would pass. Both versions run successfully; only the correlated one checks each
customer's own orders.
Find absence without a nullable-list trap
SELECT c.customer_id, c.customer_name
FROM course.customers AS c
WHERE NOT EXISTS (
SELECT 1 FROM course.orders AS o
WHERE o.customer_id = c.customer_id
ORDER BY c.customer_id;
Only C05 Tara remains. O106's null customer_id does not match Tara or any other known
customer. Unlike a nullable NOT IN list, this matching query gives a definite answer about
whether a known customer's order exists. Missing outer keys still deserve a declared policy; this
outer table has non-null primary keys, so that ambiguity is avoided here.
“Has no orders” and “has no paid orders” are different. The first accepts only Tara. The second
would accept Ravi, Mina and Tara: Ravi has an unpaid order, Mina an unknown-payment order,
and Tara none. Not having evidence of a paid order does not prove a customer has never paid
under a wider historical dataset.
A scalar correlated result
SELECT c.customer_id,
(SELECT COUNT(*) FROM course.orders AS o
WHERE o.customer_id = c.customer_id) AS order_count
FROM course.customers AS c
ORDER BY c.customer_id;
C01 through C05 have counts 2, 1, 1, 1 and 0. COUNT produces one scalar per outer customer.
A non-aggregate inner query selecting order_id would return two rows for Asha and fail in that
scalar position. Do not choose one arbitrary ID with LIMIT unless the business request specifies
which order, with a deterministic ordering rule.
Debugging and recovery
First test the inner logic with one explicit customer ID, then restore the correlation. Check a
customer with multiple matches and one with none. If everybody passes EXISTS, inspect for
missing correlation. If nobody passes an exclusion using NOT IN, check whether the subquery
contains NULL. Understand the output shape before optimising the query.
Your independent practice
Return known customers with no known-paid orders. Keep one row per customer. State why
Mina belongs in this result but should not automatically be labelled an unpaid customer.
Changed retry - after your first review
Find customers with at least two orders using a scalar correlated COUNT. Return ID and name,
one row per customer. Explain why the count cannot be replaced by EXISTS alone.
Ready-made revision
A correlated subquery uses the current outer record. EXISTS preserves outer grain while testing
any match; NOT EXISTS tests no match. Check that correlation is present and that absence
means exactly what the business sentence says. A scalar position requires one value, not an
arbitrary list of records.
Evidence to keep: your attempt, the observed result and its explanation. Save the first attempt before
opening DE03-06 in the Explained Reviews book. After review, solve the changed retry and keep it as a
separate attempt.
Before starting: DE03-06. Video: Instructor watch ranges appear below. Read the vocabulary, perform
the guided example and save an independent attempt before review.
Instructor demonstration: Learn SQL Beginner to Advanced in Under 4 Hours, 01:58:55-02:09:07. Watch CTE
structure. Use our PostgreSQL query; naming a step does not automatically materialize it. Stop manually at the
listed end. Public YouTube title, creator, runtime and expanded publisher chapter list inspected. No full-playback
or transcript-completeness claim.
Why this matters, and what you will do
A correct transformation is easier to review when its steps have names. You will total item lines
to order grain, attach those totals to every order, and add each order's shipping fee once.
Complete DE03-06. This resolves the fee multiplication measured in DE03-02.
A common table expression, or CTE, is a named query result introduced with WITH for the
duration of one statement. A later part of that statement can read the name as a table-like
input. It is not automatically a permanent table or a guarantee that PostgreSQL stores an
intermediate copy. Picture labelling a tray “item totals by order” so the next calculation can
refer to it clearly.
Follow with me once: inspect the first stage
WITH item_totals AS (
SELECT order_id,
SUM(quantity * unit_price) AS item_gross
FROM course.order_items
GROUP BY order_id
SELECT * FROM item_totals ORDER BY order_id;
There are five rows: O101 129, O102 25, O103 100, O104 250 and O105 110. The CTE's grain is
one row per order represented in the item source. Its values total 614. O106 is absent because it
has no lines. The name item_totals exists only within this one statement ending at the
semicolon.
Follow with me once: preserve order headers
WITH item_totals AS (
SELECT order_id,
SUM(quantity * unit_price) AS item_gross
FROM course.order_items
GROUP BY order_id
SELECT o.order_id,
COALESCE(i.item_gross, 0) AS item_gross,
o.shipping_fee,
COALESCE(i.item_gross, 0) + o.shipping_fee AS order_gross
FROM course.orders AS o
LEFT JOIN item_totals AS i ON o.order_id = i.order_id
ORDER BY o.order_id;
The final grain is one row per order, all six preserved. The missing joined item total means there
were no item rows for O106 in this complete classroom fixture. Under the task's rule, an empty
order has zero item gross. That is why COALESCE to zero is justified here. In an incomplete
delivery, no lines might mean “not received yet”; the same fallback could be misleading. A
transformation must know its input completeness rule.
Prove the repaired total
The six order_gross values total 664. The independent source totals are 614 from item amounts
and 50 from order fees, also 664. The raw joined calculation from DE03-02 would have produced
689 by multiplying fees. Correcting the final number is not enough: the output must also contain
six unique order IDs, including O106.
You can add a second CTE after the first, separated by a comma, then query the final step. Each
step should have a grain sentence and a checkable purpose. Avoid putting a semicolon after the
first CTE definition because that would end the statement before the consuming SELECT.
Readability does not automatically mean speed
PostgreSQL can inline or materialise CTEs depending on the query and circumstances. A CTE's
first benefit here is explainability and a deliberate transformation boundary. DE03-13 introduces
EXPLAIN; do not claim that a query is faster just because you put WITH at the front. Avoid
repeating the same long calculation across many branches when one named step makes its rule
clear.

Why this matters, and what you will do
A category total is useful, but sometimes you want to display each sale beside its category total.
GROUP BY would collapse the sale detail. You will use a window aggregate to keep each row
while adding a related summary. Complete DE03-07.
A window function calculates across a group of related rows while leaving the original result
rows available. OVER defines that window. PARTITION BY divides the rows into independent
groups for the window calculation. A frame selects which rows within a partition contribute to a
particular ordered aggregate. Picture each sale carrying a small card showing its category's
total without being merged into a single category receipt.
Follow with me once
SELECT order_id, category,
quantity * unit_price AS gross_amount,
SUM(quantity * unit_price)
OVER (PARTITION BY category) AS category_gross
FROM course.sales
ORDER BY category, order_id;
There are still eight output rows. Paper rows 0007, 0009 and 0011 each display category_gross
184. Their gross_amount values remain 99, 25 and 60. Writing's three rows each show 140;
Bags shows 250 and Tools 40. GROUP BY category would have returned four rows instead.
Window PARTITION BY establishes a calculation group, not a new output grain by itself.
Do not add the repeated category_gross column down this detailed result to produce a grand
total. Paper's 184 appears three times, so that would multiply the category summary. This is the
same grain discipline you learned with shipping fees, now applied to an intentional window
output.
Calculate a share with a declared denominator
SELECT order_id,
ROUND(100.0 * quantity * unit_price
/ NULLIF(SUM(quantity * unit_price)
OVER (PARTITION BY category), 0), 2)
AS pct_of_category
FROM course.sales
WHERE category = 'Paper'
ORDER BY order_id;
Paper shares are 53.80, 13.59 and 32.61 percent. The 100.0 converts a fraction into a
percentage while preserving numeric arithmetic. NULLIF protects a zero denominator. Rounding
individual shares can make their displayed sum differ slightly from 100 in other data; validate
the unrounded quantities if that occurs.
WHERE is logically applied before window calculations. Filtering to Paper is harmless here
because the desired partition is Paper. But if you filter to only order_id = '0007' before the
window, the partition contains just that row and its share becomes 100%. To compute the share
over all Paper rows and then show one sale, use a CTE containing the window calculation
followed by an outer filter.
A running total needs an order and a frame
SELECT order_id, ordered_on,
quantity * unit_price AS gross_amount,
SUM(quantity * unit_price) OVER (
ORDER BY ordered_on, order_id
ROWS BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW
) AS running_gross
FROM course.sales
ORDER BY ordered_on, order_id;
The running totals are 99, 129, 154, 214, 274, 324, 364 and 614. UNBOUNDED PRECEDING
means start at the first row; CURRENT ROW means stop at this row. ROWS uses individual
ordered rows. The ID resolves same-date ties. The window ORDER BY controls the calculation
sequence, while the final ORDER BY controls display. We write both explicitly.
Without a deliberate frame, the default ordered frame can include peer rows sharing an ordering
value, making a running result jump over a whole tied date. Do not memorise a frame as
punctuation; explain which rows should contribute to each result.

ordered frame defines contributing rows. WHERE affects rows before the window. Use an outer
query to filter after computing a full-population window. Repeated partition totals are not
additive detail measures.

Why this matters, and what you will do
You will choose a highest-value sale, handle equal amounts honestly, and compare consecutive
records without a self-join. Complete DE03-08. These operations are useful in latest-record
selection, deduplication policies and change analysis, but each needs an explicit ordering rule.
ROW_NUMBER assigns a different sequence number to every row in a partition. RANK gives
ties the same position and leaves gaps afterwards. DENSE_RANK gives ties the same position
without gaps. LAG reads a prior row's value in the specified order; LEAD reads a following row's
value. “Previous” means previous row in that order, not automatically previous calendar day.
Follow with me once: ties are a business decision
Use the retry sales because R201 and R203 both have gross amount 75:
SELECT order_id, quantity * unit_price AS gross_amount,
ROW_NUMBER() OVER (
ORDER BY quantity * unit_price DESC, order_id
) AS row_position,
RANK() OVER (
ORDER BY quantity * unit_price DESC
) AS amount_rank,
DENSE_RANK() OVER (
ORDER BY quantity * unit_price DESC
) AS dense_amount_rank
FROM course.retry_sales
ORDER BY gross_amount DESC, order_id;
The ROW_NUMBER includes order_id to choose a deterministic sequence within the amount tie.
RANK and DENSE_RANK deliberately rank by amount alone, so the tied 75 values share a rank. If
you added the unique ID to their window ordering too, you would break the amount tie and
change their meaning. Tie-breaking for presentation and tie-definition for ranking are different
choices.
Filter a computed ranking in the next stage
WITH ranked AS (
SELECT order_id, category, quantity * unit_price AS amount,
ROW_NUMBER() OVER (
PARTITION BY category
ORDER BY quantity * unit_price DESC, order_id
) AS rn
FROM course.sales
SELECT order_id, category, amount
FROM ranked WHERE rn = 1
ORDER BY category;
One highest sale per category appears: Bags 0014/250, Paper 0007/99, Tools 0013/40 and
Writing 0010/60. The outer WHERE can use rn because the CTE has already produced it. Trying
to filter a window function directly in the same SELECT's WHERE would violate the logical stage
order. If the business wants all equal highest sales, use an amount RANK and filter rank 1
instead of choosing one row.
Follow with me once: adjacent records
SELECT order_id, ordered_on,
quantity * unit_price AS amount,
LAG(quantity * unit_price) OVER (
ORDER BY ordered_on, order_id
) AS previous_amount,
LEAD(quantity * unit_price) OVER (
ORDER BY ordered_on, order_id
) AS next_amount
FROM course.practice_sales
ORDER BY ordered_on, order_id;
P101 has previous NULL and next 80; P102 has previous 18 and next 30; P103 has previous 80
and next 120; P104 has previous 30 and next NULL. P101 and P102 occur on the same date, so
the previous record is not the previous day. If you need day-over-day change, aggregate to one
row per day first, handle missing days according to the requirement, and then apply LAG.
A missing prior value can mean no prior row or a null value in that prior row. If the distinction
matters, also lag the prior row's key. Avoid replacing all such nulls with zero without a defined
baseline rule.

Why this matters, and what you will do
This lesson brings the engineering risk into one complete report. You will return one row per
customer region, count orders, add item gross and shipping fees once, retain the
unknown-customer bucket and compute an average at the correct grain. Complete DE03-09. A
query can use advanced syntax and still multiply money; grain remains the first decision.
Multi-grain reasoning means following measures as records move between different levels of
detail. A weighted average uses the appropriate quantity as its weight rather than giving
every summary row equal importance. A reconciliation contract names totals and counts
expected to agree across equivalent scopes.
Draw the grain changes in words
Item lines start at (order_id, line_no). They first become one item summary per order_id. Order
headers already have one row per order_id and supply shipping_fee once. Customers supply
region at one row per customer_id. The joined order-level result can finally be grouped to one
row per region. Each step has an explicit key; a field's name alone does not tell you whether it is
safe to add.
Follow with me once
WITH item_totals AS (
SELECT order_id, SUM(quantity * unit_price) AS item_gross
FROM course.order_items GROUP BY order_id
), order_totals AS (
SELECT o.order_id, c.region,
COALESCE(i.item_gross, 0) AS item_gross,
o.shipping_fee,
COALESCE(i.item_gross, 0) + o.shipping_fee AS order_gross
FROM course.orders AS o
LEFT JOIN item_totals AS i ON o.order_id = i.order_id
LEFT JOIN course.customers AS c ON o.customer_id = c.customer_id
SELECT COALESCE(region, 'Unknown') AS region_group,
COUNT(*) AS order_count,
SUM(item_gross) AS item_gross,
SUM(shipping_fee) AS shipping_fees,
SUM(order_gross) AS order_gross,
ROUND(AVG(order_gross), 2) AS avg_order_gross
FROM order_totals
GROUP BY region
ORDER BY region_group;
The Unknown display label comes from missing customer identity for O106. It is not an actual
region supplied by a known customer. Our customers.region is non-null, so that provenance is
clear in this fixture. If real data also allowed missing region on a matched customer, you would
separate those two reasons when the report needed them.
Prove each level, not just the final total
At order grain, expect six rows and six distinct order IDs. Item totals sum to 614; shipping fees
sum to 50; order gross sums to 664. At region grain, four groups must still represent six orders,
with the same 614/50/664 totals. East's three orders are O101/149, O102/35 and O103/100.
Their sum is 284, which provides a hand-check inside the overall reconciliation.
A wrong join can repeat rows and still accidentally produce a correct total if some amounts are
zero. A correct grand total can also hide amounts moved into the wrong region. Therefore check
keys, group membership, empty orders, unknowns and amounts together. These are
complementary checks, not interchangeable proof.
Why an average of averages can be wrong
The overall average order gross is 664 / 6 = 110.666..., displayed as 110.67. Taking the simple
average of the four displayed region averages gives roughly 118.67 instead, because that treats
East's three orders like one equally weighted observation and can introduce rounding error too.
To combine group means, use each group's count as a weight or, more directly, sum original
group totals and divide by sum of counts. Do not average already rounded averages if the
original numerators and denominators are available.
The inclusion of O106's zero empty order is part of this task's declared denominator. If the
question were average of non-empty orders, the denominator would be five and the mean
132.80. State the population before debating which number is right.

Temporarily replace the final SELECT with SELECT * FROM order_totals ORDER BY order_id.
Inspect that intermediate grain. If one order repeats, fix the earlier join or aggregation before
touching the final GROUP BY. If a source total and a filtered report disagree, align their scope. If
an Unknown group disappears, inspect INNER versus LEFT JOIN and any right-side WHERE
predicate.

A connection identifies a server, port, database and login role. A schema is a namespace
inside one database. A qualified name includes the schema, such as course.orders. A dialect
is the particular SQL syntax and behaviour implemented by a database product. DDL, data
definition language, defines objects; DML, data manipulation language, changes stored records.
SELECT reads records.
Follow with me once: know where the query runs
SELECT current_database() AS database_name,
current_user AS role_name,
current_schema() AS default_schema;
SHOW server_version;
SHOW search_path;
On your laptop database_name should be standalone_de, while role_name is the role used for
your connection. The default_schema and search_path depend on configuration. Common
installations search a user-named schema if it exists, then public. Do not assume course is
automatically first. The authoring test engine's own database name can differ; that is not the
value you are asked to reproduce on your installed server.
search_path determines which schemas PostgreSQL searches for an unqualified object name.
If two schemas each contain orders, FROM orders may select a different table when the search
path changes. FROM course.orders makes the intended schema explicit. A schema prefix does
not cross into another database; you choose a different database through the connection.
Inspect types without guessing from formatting
SELECT column_name, data_type, is_nullable
FROM information_schema.columns
WHERE table_schema = 'course' AND table_name = 'orders'
ORDER BY ordinal_position;
information_schema exposes standard metadata about database objects. Metadata means
information describing data: column names, types and nullability in this case. Expect order_id
text/non-null, customer_id text/nullable, ordered_on date/non-null, shipping_fee
numeric/non-null and is_paid boolean/nullable. The returned type name numeric does not itself
show the chosen precision and scale; those have their own metadata fields.
IDs are text because arithmetic does not describe their role and leading zeros may matter.
quantity uses integer because fractional notebooks are not valid in this fixture. unit_price uses
numeric(10,2): a decimal type with ten total digits and two fractional digits. A type restricts
representation, but a sensible range may also need a constraint. An integer quantity could be
negative without a separate rule.
Make one disposable table and explain every part
A temporary table belongs to your database session and normally disappears when that
session ends. It is useful for a small isolated experiment. Use this unique name in a fresh Query
Tool session:
CREATE TEMP TABLE desk_note (
note_id text PRIMARY KEY,
note_text text NOT NULL
INSERT INTO desk_note (note_id, note_text)
VALUES ('N01', 'A SQL file is saved text.');
SELECT note_id, note_text FROM desk_note;
CREATE defines the columns. PRIMARY KEY declares a non-null unique identity. NOT NULL
requires a value. INSERT supplies one record, naming the target columns to make their order
clear. SELECT reads it. The result is N01 with the sentence shown. These actions differ: saving
the script creates a file, executing CREATE creates a database object, and executing INSERT
stores a record in that object.
If you rerun CREATE in the same session, “already exists” is expected. Inspect the existing
temporary table or use a new temporary name. Do not drop course.orders to fix an unrelated
temporary-table experiment. Keeping setup, transformation and evidence files separately
named helps you avoid executing a destructive setup command by accident.

Why this matters, and what you will do
A reliable database should reject impossible records, and a multi-step change should not stop
halfway with a misleading state. You will enforce a simple data contract and practise both
committing and rolling back changes in temporary tables. Complete DE03-11. This lesson uses
disposable objects; it does not ask you to alter the master sales source.
A constraint is a rule enforced by the database. PRIMARY KEY enforces a unique non-null
identity. FOREIGN KEY requires a non-null reference to match an allowed key in another table.
CHECK tests a condition, and NOT NULL explicitly forbids missing values. A transaction groups
statements into a unit: COMMIT accepts their changes, while ROLLBACK cancels uncommitted
changes in that transaction.
Follow with me once: write the contract into a table
CREATE TEMP TABLE stock_contract (
product_id text PRIMARY KEY,
units integer NOT NULL CHECK (units >= 0)
INSERT INTO stock_contract VALUES ('PEN', 10), ('BAG', 4);
SELECT * FROM stock_contract ORDER BY product_id;
BAG/4 and PEN/10 should appear. The constraints encode distinct rules: each product ID
identifies one record, units must be supplied, and units cannot be negative. CHECK alone is not
a replacement for NOT NULL because PostgreSQL accepts a check condition that evaluates to
unknown; the explicit NOT NULL closes that gap.
Run this deliberately invalid statement by itself. It should fail with a check-constraint violation;
no NEG record should be inserted.
INSERT INTO stock_contract VALUES ('NEG', -1);
The number 23514 is PostgreSQL's SQLSTATE for this error class, not part of the query. A
duplicate product ID should trigger a unique violation; a null units value should trigger a not-null
violation. Constraints are useful because they reject the bad write rather than hoping every later
report notices it.
Follow with me once: rehearse a change and cancel it
BEGIN;
UPDATE stock_contract SET units = units - 2
WHERE product_id = 'PEN';
SELECT * FROM stock_contract WHERE product_id = 'PEN';
ROLLBACK;
SELECT * FROM stock_contract WHERE product_id = 'PEN';
Inside the transaction you see PEN/8. After ROLLBACK, you see PEN/10 again. UPDATE changes
existing records selected by WHERE. Without WHERE, every record would be updated, which
would be a different operation. Previewing the intended record with SELECT before modifying it
is a sensible habit.
ROLLBACK cancels changes still uncommitted in the current transaction. It is not an undo button
for changes committed yesterday. If pgAdmin auto-commits a standalone UPDATE, that change
is already committed unless you began an explicit transaction. This is why the lesson writes
BEGIN and ROLLBACK visibly.
Atomicity: the whole unit succeeds or is cancelled
Imagine transferring two units between two stock records. One decrease and one increase
belong together. Atomicity means that the unit is accepted together or rolled back; the
intermediate half-transfer must not be mistaken for a final state. Consistency here means
declared constraints still hold. Isolation concerns what concurrent transactions can observe,
and durability concerns accepted changes surviving normal failures. Those four terms form
ACID. This small one-session exercise demonstrates commit/rollback and constraint
enforcement, not all concurrent-isolation behaviour.
Try an explicit transaction containing a valid update and then the invalid negative insert. After
the failed statement, PostgreSQL marks that transaction aborted. Later ordinary statements fail
until ROLLBACK. Run ROLLBACK alone to recover; the earlier uncommitted update is cancelled
too. Do not keep executing unrelated queries in the aborted transaction and treat each resulting
error as a new independent problem.
Foreign keys preserve relationships, not every business rule
course.order_items.order_id references course.orders.order_id. A non-null item order ID must
correspond to an order header. Nullable customer_id on orders still allows an unidentified
customer; a foreign key does not automatically require a value. Nor does it prove that a
recorded payment is true, a product description is accurate, or an imported source is complete.
Constraints enforce the rules you actually declared.

Ready-made revision

automatically forbid NULL. BEGIN opens a transaction, COMMIT accepts it and ROLLBACK
cancels its uncommitted work. Recover an aborted transaction with ROLLBACK and then fix the

Why this matters, and what you will do
A query that works on eight records may perform poorly on a much larger table. You will inspect
a query plan, create one targeted index in a temporary experiment and compare what
PostgreSQL chooses. Complete DE03-12. Correct results come first; optimisation must preserve
the same question and records.
An index is an extra data structure that can help locate rows without scanning every table row.
A query plan describes the operations the engine intends to use. A sequential scan inspects
the table; an index scan uses an index path. Selectivity describes how narrowly a condition
filters the source. Statistics help the planner estimate result sizes and costs.
Picture a book's index: looking up one rare topic may be quicker through page references.
Reading almost the entire book may be easier in page order. Maintaining the index also takes
space and work when the book changes. Database indexes likewise are not a free universal
speed button.
Follow with me once: build an isolated experiment
CREATE TEMP TABLE plan_orders AS
SELECT n AS order_no,
n % 100 AS customer_no,
n * 1.0 AS amount
FROM generate_series(1, 10000) AS g(n);
ANALYZE plan_orders;
EXPLAIN SELECT order_no, amount
FROM plan_orders WHERE order_no = 8765;
CREATE TABLE AS stores a query's result as a table. generate_series supplies integers 1 through
10000; g(n) names the generated source and its column. The % operator gives the remainder,
producing repeated customer numbers for a later comparison. ANALYZE collects table statistics.
It is unrelated to a business analysis report despite sharing the word.
Before an index exists on order_no, expect a sequential scan with a filter. The exact text, cost
numbers and timings depend on engine version, configuration and machine. The count estimate
should be inspected as an estimate, not copied into evidence as an actual measured row count.
CREATE INDEX plan_orders_order_no_idx ON plan_orders(order_no);
ANALYZE plan_orders;
EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS)
SELECT order_no, amount
FROM plan_orders WHERE order_no = 8765;
The planner may now select an index path for this narrow equality query. EXPLAIN ANALYZE
actually executes the SELECT and adds measured observations. BUFFERS reports buffer activity.
The result query itself returns order_no 8765 and amount 8765; EXPLAIN displays plan
information instead of that ordinary data grid. Run the SELECT separately to verify correctness.
Read only the plan facts you understand
Look for the scan type, filter or index condition, estimated rows versus actual rows, and the
actual number of loops. Cost units are planner units, not milliseconds. Actual time is measured
for this execution, not a guaranteed production latency. Cache state and timing overhead can
affect a small benchmark. A native Windows server may choose or time the plan differently from
the author's PostgreSQL WASM test engine.
EXPLAIN without ANALYZE plans a statement without executing its data operation. EXPLAIN
ANALYZE does execute it. Do not casually apply ANALYZE to an UPDATE or DELETE that you did
not intend to run. Here we use SELECT against a temporary fixture only.
Compare a broad request
EXPLAIN SELECT order_no, amount
FROM plan_orders WHERE order_no >= 1;
Every row matches, so a sequential scan may be the efficient choice even though an index
exists. Its presence does not force use. Indexes also need storage and maintenance during
inserts, updates and deletes. Choose them for an observed workload, then validate both the
result and the plan. An eight-row teaching table usually gives too little evidence for a serious
performance claim.
If you are stuck
An “already exists” error can mean you reran the temporary setup in the same session. Use a
fresh Query Tool session for a clean experiment rather than modifying the course's permanent
tables. If an index does not appear in a plan, inspect selectivity, statistics and what the query
actually asks. Do not disable sequential scans just to obtain the plan shape you hoped to see.
Your independent practice
Inspect the query for order_no = 4321 after the guided index exists. Save its SELECT result and

claiming that a single run proves production speed.

Ready-made revision
Indexes offer access paths with storage and write costs. EXPLAIN shows a plan; EXPLAIN
ANALYZE executes and measures. Compare estimated and actual rows, but do not read planner
cost as milliseconds. Check a narrow and a broad query, preserve correctness, and report what
your environment actually did.

Why this matters, and what you will do
You now have a useful order-total calculation. Several reports might need it. You will give that
calculation a reusable database name, understand when its results are computed, and
distinguish a view from a stored snapshot. Complete DE03-13.
A view stores a query definition and exposes its result through a table-like name. An ordinary
view does not store a separate durable copy of the result rows. A materialized view stores
results and needs a deliberate refresh to bring them up to date. A CTE names a result only
within one statement; a view remains as a database object until removed, subject to its scope
and permissions. We create temporary views here so the experiment stays within the current
session.
Follow with me once
CREATE TEMP VIEW order_totals_view AS
WITH item_totals AS (
SELECT order_id, SUM(quantity * unit_price) AS item_gross
FROM course.order_items GROUP BY order_id
SELECT o.order_id, o.customer_id, o.is_paid,
COALESCE(i.item_gross, 0) AS item_gross,
o.shipping_fee,
COALESCE(i.item_gross, 0) + o.shipping_fee AS order_gross
FROM course.orders AS o
LEFT JOIN item_totals AS i ON o.order_id = i.order_id;
SELECT order_id, order_gross
FROM order_totals_view ORDER BY order_id;
The six totals remain O101 149, O102 35, O103 100, O104 265, O105 115 and O106 0. You can
now query order_totals_view without retyping its entire definition. Its contract is still one row per
order with the same complete-fixture rule for empty orders. The convenient name does not
remove the need to validate its logic.
SELECT COUNT(*) AS orders,
COUNT(DISTINCT order_id) AS distinct_orders,
SUM(order_gross) AS gross
FROM order_totals_view;
Expect 6, 6 and 664. These checks belong to the view's contract and can be reused after a
change. A view is not automatically a security boundary or performance improvement.
Permissions and execution details need their own design, taught more deeply later.
Show that an ordinary view reads current underlying data
Use a separate tiny temporary table so the main training records remain intact:
CREATE TEMP TABLE view_source (code text, units integer);
INSERT INTO view_source VALUES ('A', 2);
CREATE TEMP VIEW view_demo AS
SELECT code, units, units * 10 AS value FROM view_source;
SELECT * FROM view_demo;
UPDATE view_source SET units = 3 WHERE code = 'A';
SELECT * FROM view_demo;
Before the update, the view returns A/2/20; after it, A/3/30. You did not refresh an ordinary view
or edit its stored result because it represents a query over the current source. A materialized
view would retain its stored result until refreshed; a historical CSV export would also remain an
old snapshot until regenerated.
A stable contract is more than a convenient name
Downstream queries can depend on the view's column names, types, meanings and grain.
Changing order_gross from fee-inclusive to item-only without changing its contract would
silently mislead those readers. CREATE OR REPLACE VIEW can update a definition within
PostgreSQL's permitted compatibility rules, but replacing syntax does not substitute for
reviewing the meaning change. Keep a clear definition and validate existing consumers when a
shared view changes.
A view definition should not be relied on to force final display order. The query reading it should
use its own ORDER BY. Likewise, selecting a subset of its columns does not remove the
underlying rule that determines its rows.
If you are stuck
If a temporary view disappears in another Query Tool tab, remember that it belongs to its
creating session. Run its creation script in the session where you want to use it. If you need a
persistent shared view later, create it in a deliberately chosen schema with appropriate
permissions; do not assume the temporary tutorial object was permanent. If rows duplicate,
investigate the definition rather than adding DISTINCT at every consumer.
Your independent practice
Query order_totals_view for known-unpaid orders, retaining empty orders. Return ID and gross,
then count those orders and sum their gross. State why a count of one would be wrong even if
the amount still looked right.

transaction's visible source state.
Ready-made revision
An ordinary view stores a query definition, a materialized view stores results, and a CTE is
scoped to one statement. Temporary views are session-scoped. Publish clear grain, meaning,
field and null-handling contracts; test counts and totals. A reusable name does not guarantee
correctness, security, ordering or speed.

What this lesson measures
You have learned the component skills. Now you will combine them on a new fictional delivery
with different amounts, repeated fees and an empty order. Complete DE03-14. This is a
practical challenge, so do not watch a solution video first. If a skill needs refreshing, revisit its
earlier assigned segment, record that help and then begin a fresh attempt. There is no new
syntax hidden in the task.
Run labs/SQL/01_load_assessments.sql once on your standalone_de database after the initial
load. It creates assessment inputs without solutions. If the tables already exist, inspect them
rather than rerunning the loader; use the setup guide's recovery instructions if a failed load left
a transaction open. The course reset removes these assessment tables too, so after a deliberate
reset both load files need to be rerun in order.
Understand the new delivery
Use course.challenge_customers, course.challenge_orders and course.challenge_items.
Customer grain is customer_id, order grain is order_id, and item grain is (order_id, line_no).
There is no item name because this task needs quantity and price, not product classification. A
missing customer_id stays unknown. An order with no item rows is an intentionally empty order
in this complete fixture, so its item amount is zero while its actual fee still counts.
Read the inputs with SELECT statements and save their counts. This is permitted preparation;
the challenge is constructing and validating the transformation rather than guessing unseen
source values. Do not open the matching Explained Reviews section until your attempt is saved.
A method you can follow without an answer
First write one sentence for the desired final grain. Name each amount's source grain before
deciding where it can be added. Build and inspect the item summary alone, then the order-level
result, and only then the final summary. Keep an empty-order case visible. Finally, check
independent totals from the original tables so a mistake in the same prepared result does not
validate itself.
A helpful help-request format is: “DE03-15, I expect one row per order; my intermediate query
returns ..., and I think the mismatch begins at ...”. Include the SQL and actual output. This gives
your tutor something concrete to diagnose and makes the amount of assistance visible.
Your independent practice
Save DE03-15_attempt.sql with numbered queries and a short evidence file.
1. Build one row per order with item_gross, shipping_fee, order_gross, customer_id and all three
payment states preserved. Keep every order, including the empty one.
2. Return one row per region, displaying Unknown for missing customer identity. Include
order_count and order_gross. Reconcile the count, item amount, fees and final amount to their
original sources.
3. Return every order tied for highest order_gross within its region. Preserve ties by amount
rather than arbitrarily choosing one. Explain the difference from ROW_NUMBER.
4. Identify customers with no orders. Explain why this is different from customers with no paid
orders.
5. Explain why SUM(DISTINCT shipping_fee) is unsafe on this delivery. Use the actual repeated
fee values as evidence.
Before review, record what you could solve independently, any help used and the remaining
uncertainty. A query that executes but loses an order or misclassifies a payment is not ready
merely because the totals look plausible.
Changed retry - after your first review
Use course.challenge_retry_customers, course.challenge_retry_orders and
course.challenge_retry_items. Build all-order totals and region totals from a blank editor. Keep
empty orders and unknown identity, reconcile counts and amounts, and calculate the average
gross per order over the complete order population. Explain why averaging region averages
equally would be unsafe. Do not reuse the previous result numbers.
Ready-made revision
For an unfamiliar source, inspect its fields and grain before writing the final report. Construct a
validated order-level result, then summarise or rank it. Empty orders may still have fees.
Repeated equal fees are legitimate on different orders. Save evidence of independence and
repair, not just a polished final query.

What this lesson measures
An interview adds communication and limited time to the SQL skills you have practised. You will
explain assumptions, solve a small set of questions and review accuracy before speed.
Complete DE03-15 and its changed retry. A stopwatch is an optional measurement tool for this
rehearsal, not a forced study timer or an automatic mastery switch.
First attempt the set untimed if time pressure makes it hard to think. When you can solve it
independently, repeat a changed set with a 45-minute total budget: five minutes to inspect the
task, thirty to write and run queries, and ten to validate and explain. Those times are a practice
arrangement, not a universal employer format. Record actual time and help used; finishing
quickly does not compensate for wrong grain or lost unknowns.
How to talk while solving
Start with the question in plain language: “One output row per customer; dates choose recency;
ID breaks same-date ties.” State any ambiguity before committing to a query. Explain a small
plan, then type. If an error appears, identify the stage or missing assumption instead of
apologising repeatedly. A useful explanation tells the interviewer why the result is correct, not
only which SQL keywords you remember.
You may consult table definitions and your own prior work during the untimed learning attempt.
For the timed rehearsal, use only the supplied source definitions, your query editor and its error
messages. If you open an answer, label that portion assisted and repair it later on the changed
set. This book does not award an external interview pass from a self-reported timer.
Your independent practice
Use the original course.sales, course.customers, course.orders and course.order_items tables.
Save one .sql file with four numbered answers and a brief spoken-or-written explanation for
each.
1. From course.sales, return the latest sale per known customer, with date descending and
order_id descending as the tie-breaker. Exclude missing customer identity explicitly. Keep one
record per known customer.
2. From course.sales, show categories with at least two sales and gross total above 150. State
the input and output grain and why the conditions use HAVING.
3. From orders and order_items, return all orders with item_gross and fee-inclusive order_gross,
preserving empty orders. Supply an independent amount reconciliation and a unique-order
check.
4. Diagnose this claim: “COUNT(is_paid) counts paid orders, and adding DISTINCT after a join
always prevents duplicate money.” Give one concrete counterexample for each using the
course data.
At the end, choose the least certain query and explain a specific changed input that would test
it. Do not quietly repair your saved first attempt after reading the review; save the repair
separately.
